clue.text: Monsieur enters to have a little soup

parts.note: to have someone, in the sense of tricking them, is to con them

indicators.note: Someone who enters a room ends up inside it, so the letter arrives in the middle of the word beside it rather than alongside.

parts.note: a little of something is some of it, and the Frenchman's letter goes in among these four
M is the standard abbreviation for the French courtesy title, as written on an envelope

explanation.walkthrough: 'to have' looks like joinery holding the sentence up; it is the first chunk of the wordplay, in the sense of having someone over.
explanation.definitionFit: soup -> CONSOMME: a clear broth simmered from meat stock and served as a first course, so the general word names one particular dish.

clue.text: Bit of wind taking the wings off two Boeings

indicators.note: Wings are the outer edges of a thing, so stripping them leaves only what was sitting in the middle of the words.

parts.note: four consecutive letters run across the join between these two words once the outer ones are gone

explanation.walkthrough: Boeing builds aeroplanes, so 'wings' reads as part of the picture rather than as an instruction. The aircraft never matter; only the spelling does.
explanation.definitionFit: Bit of wind -> OBOE: an instrument sounded by blowing, so it belongs to the wind section of an orchestra and 'bit of' picks out one member.

clue.text: Son worked on boat up the creek

parts.note: S is the standard abbreviation for son, as on a family tree
the hands who work a boat are its crew, and as a verb they crewed her

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a lad helping out on the water. 'Up the creek' is the short form of being up it without a paddle, which is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: up the creek -> SCREWED: both are idioms for being stuck in hopeless trouble with no way out, the answer being the blunter modern one.

clue.text: Rug on top for Spooner? Surely not

indicators.note: the clue asks for the phrase as Spooner would say it, swapping the opening sounds of two words

parts.note: something on top is high up
a rug is a mat

explanation.surface: A question about whether a toupee counts as a hat, answered with mock disbelief.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rug on top' gives HIGH MAT; 'for Spooner' swaps the opening sounds, as the Reverend Spooner did, giving MY HAT.
explanation.definitionFit: 'My hat!' is an old exclamation of astonishment, much like saying 'Surely not!'

clue.text: Shortened horsy draught animal's 12 hour day

indicators.note: shortened means the word loses its last letter, cutting it short

parts.note: equine means relating to horses
an ox is an animal used for pulling ploughs and carts

explanation.surface: A description of a rather horse-like animal that pulls a cart.
explanation.definitionFit: At an equinox the sun is over the equator, so day and night each last about twelve hours.

clue.text: Really enjoy Alien in which ship's beginning to dissolve with acid

indicators.note: The clue says the vessel's letter is in the creature, so that letter is planted between its two rather than added on the end.

parts.note: to dig something, in sixties slang, is to be very keen on it

indicators.note: A word's beginning is the letter it opens with, so only that one is taken from the vessel.

parts.note: ET is the crossword's standard alien, short for extraterrestrial
the first letter of ship, the vessel the surface has in mind

explanation.walkthrough: Italics mark Alien as the film, which is scene-setting only. The wordplay wants the two-letter alien every crossword uses, and a spacecraft is just a ship.
explanation.definitionFit: dissolve with acid -> DIGEST: the stomach breaks food down in acid, and that is precisely the process this verb names.

clue.text: Scoffing expert finally said "That is an old master"

indicators.note: Finally points at the end of the word beside it, so only its closing letter is taken.

parts.note: the closing letter of said
i.e. is short for the Latin id est, which translates as that is
Titian was the great Venetian painter of the sixteenth century, one of the old masters

explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks make the last five words sound like someone admiring a painting on a wall; the wordplay reads them piece by piece instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Scoffing expert -> DIETITIAN: scoff is British slang for eating greedily, so the scoffing expert is the professional who advises on what people eat.

clue.text: Burning light alarmingly close in space

indicators.note: A thing said to be in another sits among its letters, so the piece just clued is dropped into the middle of the one that follows.

parts.note: a gap is the space left between two things
to slam a door is to close it hard enough to make everyone jump

explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures two objects nearly colliding out in the cosmos. 'Close' is not a distance at all but a door being shut, and 'space' is only a gap.
explanation.definitionFit: Burning light -> GAS LAMP: a lamp with a live flame inside it, so unlike a bulb this kind of light really is burning.

clue.text: Acting independently troubled Nelson a tad

indicators.note: troubled means disturbed and thrown into disorder, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Admiral Nelson, a little worried, going it alone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'troubled' tells you to rearrange the letters of NELSON, A and TAD.
explanation.definitionFit: Something standalone operates on its own, without support or connection to anything else.

clue.text: Trying venue where race might be held that accommodates 1,000

indicators.note: To accommodate guests is to house them within your walls, so the number named next goes inside the letters already clued.

parts.note: a race is run over a course, whether the runners are horses or people
thou is the everyday short form of a thousand

explanation.walkthrough: 'Trying' is the pun: not wearisome but conducting a trial. The surface keeps you at the racetrack, where the same word would mean a testing afternoon.
explanation.definitionFit: Trying venue -> COURTHOUSE: the building where trials are heard, so 'trying' is the legal verb at work rather than the tiring adjective.

clue.text: Anorak's over fleece

indicators.note: over means turned over, so the letters are read backwards

parts.note: a mac is a raincoat like an anorak, and the 's adds an S

explanation.surface: An anorak worn on top of a fleece jacket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' turns MACS (mac plus the 's) round. Fleece here is the verb, not the jacket.
explanation.definitionFit: To fleece someone is to cheat them of money, which is exactly what a swindle does.

clue.text: Wii boxing in back of tavern in Thailand, drunken comedy

indicators.note: To box something in is to shut it on every side, so the console's letters close round everything else.

parts.note: Nintendo's games console, spelled with a double i

indicators.note: The back of a word is its final letter, so one letter comes out of the tavern and no more.

parts.note: the country supplies eight letters, opened up early on to take the tavern's letter

indicators.note: The country is where the tavern's letter is put, so it lands among the letters of the name rather than beside them.

parts.note: the letter at the back of the word tavern

explanation.walkthrough: 'Drunken' looks like an instruction to shuffle and is not: it belongs to the definition, describing a 1987 film about two soaked out-of-work actors.
explanation.definitionFit: drunken comedy -> WITHNAIL AND I: Bruce Robinson's film follows two permanently sozzled actors through a wet weekend, so the definition names it by its plot.

clue.text: Get rid of husband, but shag single comedian first

indicators.note: What comes first is written at the front, so the three pieces just clued line up ahead of the letter for the spouse.

parts.note: to bed someone is the printable verb for what the surface says more coarsely
a single of anything is one of it
a wit is someone whose talk gets laughs, which is a comedian's whole trade
H is the standard abbreviation for husband, as on a form

explanation.walkthrough: The order is the trap: the husband is named at the start of the clue and written at the end of the answer, and 'but' only props the sentence up.
explanation.definitionFit: Get rid of -> BE DONE WITH: to be done with a person is to have finished with them for good, which is disposal put as a decision.

clue.text: Sponge without water perhaps upsetting Mary, die on cross

indicators.note: upsetting means knocking over and disordering, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
X is the shape of a cross

explanation.surface: A baking mishap involving Mary, a dice and a cross shape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upsetting' rearranges MARY and DIE into READYMI, and 'on' places the cross, X, after it.
explanation.definitionFit: A packet sponge mix is ready-mixed, needing only liquid added, so a dry sponge mix is one example.

clue.text: You must cut extremely long hair

indicators.note: To cut into something is to go right through the middle of it, so the letter for the reader lands inside the word that follows.

parts.note: extremely rich and most rich say the same thing, so the adverb hands over four letters
U stands in for you in text-message spelling
to long for something is to ache for it

explanation.walkthrough: 'You must cut' reads as an order barked at the solver, and that is exactly what it is — an instruction about one letter, not about anybody's hair.
explanation.definitionFit: hair -> MOUSTACHE: the definition names the general stuff and the answer is one particular growth of it, the kind worn on the upper lip.

clue.text: Stick one's china back on mantelpiece

parts.note: a person speaking of themselves turns one is into I'm, two letters once the apostrophe goes
china plate is Cockney rhyming slang for mate, and a mate is a pal

indicators.note: The back of a word is its rear end, so what is wanted from the long one is the single letter it finishes on.

parts.note: the letter this long word ends on

explanation.walkthrough: 'Stick' is the definition and it is a verb, meaning to run something through on a spike — not the noun the ornaments and the mantelpiece invite.
explanation.definitionFit: Stick -> IMPALE: to stick a fork through a piece of meat is to impale it, the verb for driving a point clean through something.

clue.text: Japanese island ducks largely avoid

parts.note: ducks is a British term of endearment, like hon (honey)

indicators.note: largely means most of the word, so its last letter is dropped

parts.note: to shun is to avoid

explanation.surface: Waterfowl on a Japanese island keeping mostly out of the way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ducks' is how some Britons address a friend ('ta, ducks'), the same as hon. 'largely' cuts SHUN to SHU.
explanation.definitionFit: Honshu is the largest of the main islands of Japan, home to Tokyo.

clue.text: Shoe reeks, case of aeration failing?

indicators.note: A case is the shell that encloses a thing, so what is taken is the pair of letters at either end of the word.
Something failing is coming apart at the seams, and letters that come apart can be reassembled in any order.

parts.note: the two letters that case this word, one at each end
five letters as printed, waiting to be reordered along with the pair beside them

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the whole picture as invention: footwear has no aeration case. It is there so 'case of' reads as a complaint rather than an order.
explanation.definitionFit: Shoe -> SNEAKER: a soft rubber-soled trainer, named for how quietly you can creep about in it, so it is one kind of shoe.

clue.text: Accurately position leg and off-side fielder

parts.note: pins is old slang for legs, as in being unsteady on them
point is the cricket fielding position square of the batter on the off side

explanation.walkthrough: Cricket divides the field into the leg side and the off side, and the clue uses both words — one as a limb, one as a genuine fielding position.
explanation.definitionFit: Accurately position -> PINPOINT: to pinpoint a target is to fix exactly where it is, the verb borrowed from marking a map with a pin.

clue.text: Half retire in style earlier than expected

indicators.note: Half of a six-letter word is three letters, and the front half is what the clue hands over.
A piece described as being in another is planted among its letters rather than added at either end.

parts.note: a perm is a hairstyle, short for permanent wave
the first half of retire, three of its six letters

explanation.walkthrough: 'Half retire' is solver's shorthand for taking half the letters, not for going part-time, and the early retirement in the surface is the joke.
explanation.definitionFit: earlier than expected -> PRETERM: a preterm baby arrives before its due date, the prefix pre- carrying exactly that sense of ahead of time.

clue.text: How to serve cheese and beans? Not with head inside oven

definitions.text: How to serve cheese and beans?

indicators.note: inside means the head letter is moved within the rest of the word

parts.note: the word not, without its first letter
the head of Not is its first letter, N
an oast is a kiln or oven for drying hops

explanation.surface: A kitchen question, answered with a warning not to put your head in the oven.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the head, N, off NOT to leave OT, and put it inside, giving ONT; add OAST, a hop-drying oven common in Kent.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheese and baked beans are classically served on a slice of toasted bread.

clue.text: Old record tied yet broken in prospect

indicators.note: A broken thing is in pieces that can be put back any way round, so the three letters beside the word are reordered.
Something in a thing lies within its letters, so the pieces assembled first are planted inside the word that follows.

parts.note: a prospect is a view, and a view is a sight
scores that are tied are level, or even
the three letters of yet, put back in another order

explanation.walkthrough: 'Record ... broken' is the surface's athletics story and has nothing to do with it: the record here is the brittle shellac disc a wind-up gramophone played.
explanation.definitionFit: Old record -> SEVENTY-EIGHT: shellac discs are named after the revolutions a minute they spin at, and collectors still call them by that number.

clue.text: Put precious coat on to cover uniform for society

indicators.note: To cover something is to lie over it on both sides, so the letter named next is taken in among the ones already clued.

parts.note: to gild is to lay a thin skin of gold over something
U is uniform in the radio alphabet, where every letter has a spoken name

explanation.walkthrough: 'Put precious coat on' is one instruction rather than three, and 'precious' is in it only because the metal being laid on has to be gold.
explanation.definitionFit: society -> GUILD: an association of craftsmen banded together to protect a trade, so it is one particular kind of society.

clue.text: Slow mover missing the last scheduled time

indicators.note: Missing the last means the final letter has gone, so the creature's name is written out one letter short.

parts.note: the sloth hangs about in South American trees and is a byword for going nowhere fast

explanation.walkthrough: The surface grumbles about a dawdler who has missed the last bus. 'The last' is not part of that story: it is an instruction about a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: scheduled time -> SLOT: the fixed gap in a timetable that a plane or a broadcast is allotted, so it names a booked stretch of time.

clue.text: Beat little pest that won't let go

definitions.meaning: a clock marks each beat of time with one small sound

definitions.text: little pest that won't let go
definitions.meaning: the parasite that buries its head in a dog's skin and cannot be shaken off

explanation.walkthrough: Nothing is anagrammed or hidden here: the clue simply sets two unrelated meanings side by side and lets the surface pretend they are one sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: Beat -> TICK: the regular beat of a clock, while the little pest is the blood-sucking mite that fastens onto skin and holds until pulled off.

clue.text: Decent plastic ID bracelet

indicators.note: Plastic means easily moulded into another shape, so the letters beside the word can be pressed into a different order.

parts.note: the ten letters of these two words, pressed into a new shape

explanation.walkthrough: 'Plastic ID bracelet' is one believable object, which is what hides the instruction inside it. The enumeration is the tell: the phrase holds exactly ten letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Decent -> CREDITABLE: work that does you credit is respectable enough to earn praise, which is what calling a performance decent amounts to.

clue.text: Bill right to replace note in coins

indicators.note: to replace means one letter takes the place of another in the word

parts.note: loose coins are change

explanation.surface: Swapping a banknote for coins to pay a bill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'right to replace note' means R takes the place of N in CHANGE.
explanation.definitionFit: A charge is a price or fee asked, and so is a bill presented for payment.

clue.text: Consider change to clue, perhaps Mike worried about it?

indicators.note: about it means going round it, the change just named, so these letters surround that piece

parts.note: M is Mike in the NATO phonetic alphabet
something that ate at you worried you
to edit is to change a text, such as a crossword clue

explanation.surface: A setter wondering whether to edit a clue that has bothered Mike.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about it' puts M and ATE around EDIT, the 'it' pointing back to the change to the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: To meditate on something is to ponder or think it over carefully.
